# Religion Across the Three Eras

## The requirement

> status: ratified (D-0008, D-0047, D-0078)

Religion here is the human relationship to the Wyrd, and it must be different in the
pre-history, the main story time, and the narrator's time — with deliberate thought
about breadth versus monolithism, and why belief changes as eras turn. The narrator
is a religious scholar of the history of the study of Wyrd and Frith, standing in a
line of religious organizations with genuinely deep understanding (Dune-flavored
institutional depth, grounded in this world's values). The world's theology must also
be discoverable inside episodes — architecture, habit, hypocrisy — not only through
the cold opens. Everything is pre-Christian Northern European in root and flavor; an
invading, standardizing faith-pressure on native belief is part of the cultural
conflict ([[the-empire]], D-0026).

## The shape of the arc

> status: proposed

The session's unratified model: **breadth → forced monolith → networked synthesis.**
In the pre-history, belief was hyper-local of necessity — every valley's spirits and
duties were its own, a vast polyculture with no possible universal church. The
empire, unable to tax a polyculture, imposed a monolith: worship of its own perfected
arithmetic in the high keeps, and criminalized fragments of animism everywhere below.
The narrator's era learned from both failures: shared core values (Frith), radically
local practice — a decentralized communion of orders that agree on the law of
reciprocity and refuse, on principle, to centralize anything else.

## Story-time faith on the ground

> status: proposed

Sketches for the main era, unratified: the state cult of the Ledger-as-divine-order,
attended by the ambitious and enforced by auditor-inquisitors; terrified folk
observance in the spokes — a miner praising the keep's arithmetic aloud, then
bleeding a quiet thumb against the shaft-wall on the way in; penitent movements
flagellating their villages for the weather ([[information-control]]); and the hunted
remnant of real practice — cunning-folk, midwives, keeners — holding rituals they can
no longer fully explain.

## The narrator's orders

> status: provisional (D-0047)

Ratified in role, provisional in texture: generations-deep religious organizations
that study the Wyrd and Frith as sacred history. The session's sketch: subterranean
bog-archives (anaerobic, preserving — see [[megaliths-and-leys]]), a suspicion of the
bound book inherited from the empire's abuses, scripture kept in weave and knot, and
scholars whose vocation is decoding the tactile records of the story's era — the
narrator among them, reading the very events we hear ([[narrator-framing]]).

## Proposed organizations, roles, documents, figures

> status: proposed

The explicit inventory requested by the author, all names unratified (Q-0002):

- *Pre-history*: a commons-guild of ecological intercessors ("threshold-weavers")
  maintaining valley-treaties; scripture as living landscape — stones, leys, woven
  records; a myth-figure remembered as the first to ground the Wyrd with iron and
  make safe hearths possible.
- *Story time*: the empire's doctrinal ministry and its auditor-inquisitors; iron-bound
  folios of quota-law treated as holy writ; underground cunning-cults improvising
  half-remembered rites; a living folk-saint — a blind midwife who carries the old
  birth-rites from camp to camp, hunted and beloved.
- *Narrator time*: the frithic monastic network and its thread-reader scholars;
  nomadic seed-keeper monks who test soils and warn any settlement growing large
  enough to need a ledger again; the great woven chronicle of the trio's era, kept as
  both sacred relic and history text; the protagonist and apprentice remembered not
  as gods but as flawed, muddy saints — "the Vessel" and "the Child of the Root."

## How the audience discovers all this

> status: proposed

Beyond the cold opens: theological archaeology in the mise-en-scène (imperial
foundations squatting on older circle-stones), doctrine glimpsed through hypocrisy
(who prays to what, when nobody official is watching), and the protagonist's Archive
itself — absorbed believers of different centuries arguing liturgy inside her skull,
overheard in fragments ([[protagonist]], [[audio-design]]).

## The turnings — a festival wheel of the parishes
> status: ratified (D-0146)

The parishes keep a festival year, and it is the world's own — never a single eightfold
calendar. Each region marks a handful of turning-points keyed to its own livelihood and its
own Wyrd — a fringe tide-turn, a crag ember-night, a lowland bog-offering — so the wheel is
local where the empire's is uniform, which is the whole quarrel between them ([[regions]]).
The rites are work and reciprocity, closer to a shared settling of accounts than a spectacle.
Song, drum, and dance belong to them as culture and as the show's score, and never as the
working magic — the music clause holds here as everywhere ([[magic-system]] "The music clause",
D-0002). The turnings carry no imported names; what each one is called awaits the naming oracle
(Q-0002), so for now they are described by what they do.

## The hearth and the iron
> status: ratified (D-0146)

Domestic faith centres on the hearth: the household's held frith, the one small commons a
family keeps in balance and tends as the house's sacred centre. Iron guards its edges — a nail
over the threshold, a blade under the doorstone, a ring on the crib — set there to ground the
Wyrd and keep the hearth safe, the daily-life heir of the myth-figure who first grounded the
Wyrd with iron ("Proposed organizations", above). This is the same iron the crags work with
such care ([[economy]], D-0123, D-0144): the protective charm and the honest craft are one
material worked in two registers, the same iron that guards a door and dignifies a hidden
joint. Those who keep the charms often no longer know why they hold ([[professions]]
"Fragment-holders"), and the fragment stays real even when the reason is lost.

## Naming the dead
> status: ratified (D-0146)

The dead are kept by being named. A community's remembrance rite is the speaking of its dead
into the record that outlasts them — their names woven into the parish register or spoken over
the bog that preserves them — so that remembrance itself becomes the act that defeats the
empire's policing of memory ([[information-control]]). This is the domestic, everyday form of
the vindication the narrator's order will embody centuries on: memory outlasts power (D-0117,
[[narrator]]). A keening may carry the grief and a drum may keep the time, but the keeping is
the naming and the weaving, never the tune (the music clause, D-0002). The keeners and skalds
who lead it hold a craft the empire calls a capital crime ([[professions]]).
